concepts.label: Population
concepts.definition: The entire set of people or items that the investigation is concerned with.
concepts.example: Every student enrolled at a particular school, if the question concerns all its students.
concepts.misconception: A population does not have to mean everyone in a country.

concepts.label: Census
concepts.definition: An investigation in which every member of the defined population is observed or measured.
concepts.example: Recording the height of every student in Year 12.
concepts.misconception: A census is not guaranteed error-free: measurements and responses can still be inaccurate.

concepts.label: Sample
concepts.definition: Observations taken from part of a population to learn about the population as a whole.
concepts.example: Recording the heights of 40 of the 200 students in Year 12.
concepts.misconception: A sample is not the same as the whole population.

concepts.label: Raw data
concepts.definition: Original observations or measurements before they have been processed or summarised.
concepts.example: A list of individually recorded travel times before calculating a mean.
concepts.misconception: A calculated mean is a summary, not raw data.

concepts.label: Sampling unit
concepts.definition: One individual member or item of a population that could be selected for a sample.
concepts.example: One pupil when the population consists of pupils.
concepts.misconception: A sampling unit is an item or person, not the list containing them.

concepts.label: Sampling frame
concepts.definition: A list or other identification system of the population's sampling units from which a sample can be selected.
concepts.example: A numbered register containing all 240 eligible pupils.
concepts.misconception: A frame may be incomplete or out of date; it is not the sample itself.

concepts.label: Random sampling
concepts.definition: Choosing sampling units by a chance-based procedure rather than the researcher's personal judgement.
concepts.example: Selecting numbered pupils by a correctly used random number generator.
concepts.misconception: Chance-based selection does not guarantee the result represents the population; equal chances of all units also depend on the design.

concepts.label: Simple random sampling
concepts.definition: Selecting a sample so that every possible group of the required size has the same probability of selection.
concepts.example: Number all 120 pupils; generate 15 distinct random numbers from 1 to 120 and select those pupils.
concepts.misconception: Equal chances for individuals alone do not fully define a simple random sample.

concepts.label: Systematic sampling
concepts.definition: Selecting units at regular intervals from an ordered list, using a random starting position.
concepts.example: From 100 numbered pupils, randomly start at 3 and then choose 3, 8, 13, ... for a sample of 20.
concepts.misconception: Selecting every fifth pupil without randomising the starting position is an incomplete procedure.

concepts.label: Stratified sampling
concepts.definition: Dividing the population into non-overlapping groups (strata) and choosing a random sample within each group.
concepts.example: For a sample of 40 from 60% Year 12 and 40% Year 13, randomly choose 24 and 16 respectively.
concepts.misconception: Dividing into groups does not make sampling stratified if people within them are not selected randomly.

concepts.label: Stratum
concepts.definition: One of the mutually exclusive groups into which a population is divided for stratified sampling.
concepts.example: The Year 12 students, when year groups are used as the strata.
concepts.misconception: A stratum is a group in the population, not a single sampling unit.

concepts.label: Quota sampling
concepts.definition: Choosing people non-randomly to fill set numbers for particular population groups.
concepts.example: Approach available students until 30 Year 12 and 20 Year 13 responses have been collected.
concepts.misconception: Matching group proportions does not make this stratified random sampling.

concepts.label: Opportunity sampling
concepts.definition: Choosing eligible people or items that are readily available when the investigation takes place.
concepts.example: Question the first 20 shoppers who agree to participate near a supermarket entrance.
concepts.misconception: Opportunity sampling is non-random, and its convenient group may not reflect the population.

concepts.label: Selection bias
concepts.definition: A systematic distortion caused when some members of the target population are more likely to be selected than others.
concepts.example: Only interviewing people using the school library at lunchtime to estimate everyone's reading habits.
concepts.misconception: Random sampling reduces some selection bias but cannot correct an incomplete sampling frame.

concepts.label: Representative sample
concepts.definition: A sample whose relevant characteristics resemble those of the population being studied.
concepts.example: The sample's proportions by year group match the school population's proportions.
concepts.misconception: Matching one characteristic does not guarantee representativeness for every other characteristic.

concepts.label: Sampling variation
concepts.definition: Differences in sample results that occur because different subsets of the same population are selected.
concepts.example: Two random samples from the same year group produce different mean journey times.
concepts.misconception: A different sample mean does not automatically imply a mistake or bias.

concepts.label: Sampling interval
concepts.definition: The regular gap between successive selections in a systematic sample.
concepts.example: For a population of 100 and sample of 20, the interval is 5.
concepts.misconception: When N divided by n is not an integer, do not invent a universal rounding rule.

concepts.label: Proportional allocation
concepts.definition: Assigning each stratum a share of the sample proportional to its share of the population.
concepts.example: A group containing 30% of the population gets 30% of the sample, subject to whole-number allocation.
concepts.misconception: Proportions determine how many to sample, not who is selected inside each stratum.

concepts.label: Qualitative data
concepts.definition: Data describing categories or qualities rather than numerical amounts.
concepts.example: Eye colour or favourite subject.
concepts.misconception: A category may be stored as a numerical code without becoming quantitative data.

concepts.label: Quantitative data
concepts.definition: Data representing numerical amounts obtained by counting or measuring.
concepts.example: Number of siblings or height in centimetres.
concepts.misconception: A numeric label such as a bus route number is not necessarily quantitative.

concepts.label: Discrete variable
concepts.definition: A variable that can take only separate, distinct values within its possible range.
concepts.example: The number of children in a household: 0, 1, 2, ...
concepts.misconception: Discrete does not necessarily mean 'whole numbers' in every context.

concepts.label: Continuous variable
concepts.definition: A variable that can take any value in a continuous interval (in the mathematical model).
concepts.example: Time to complete a race, even if the measuring instrument rounds it.
concepts.misconception: Rounded measurements do not turn an inherently continuous variable into a discrete one.

concepts.label: Grouped frequency table
concepts.definition: A frequency table in which values are collected into intervals or classes rather than listed individually.
concepts.example: Times grouped into 0 <= t < 10, 10 <= t < 20 and 20 <= t < 30 seconds.
concepts.misconception: The individual observations cannot normally be recovered exactly from grouped data.

concepts.label: Class boundaries
concepts.definition: The lower and upper values that define a class interval.
concepts.example: For 10 <= t < 20, the class boundaries are 10 and 20.
concepts.misconception: Class boundaries are not always the same as printed class limits for rounded measurements.

concepts.label: Class width
concepts.definition: The difference between the upper and lower class boundaries.
concepts.example: For a class 10 <= t < 20, class width = 20 - 10 = 10.
concepts.misconception: Do not count the number of integers in an interval when calculating its width.

concepts.label: Class midpoint
concepts.definition: The mean of the lower and upper class boundaries.
concepts.example: For a class from 10 to 20, the midpoint is (10 + 20)/2 = 15.
concepts.misconception: The class midpoint estimates values in the class; it need not be an actual observed value.
